title: Saul heard the songs before he saw the threat.
paragraphs: Saul heard the songs before he saw the threat.
The women came dancing through the streets of Israel after battle, tambourines shaking, voices rising like wildfire through the valleys:
“Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” — 1 Samuel 18:7
That single lyric shattered something inside a king.
Not because Saul lost a battle.
Because Saul realized heaven was touching someone else.

And some people can survive criticism…
but they cannot survive watching someone else carry the favor they once had.
This is the untold tragedy behind King Saul.
Not merely jealousy.
Not insecurity.
But the terror of a man watching another person become what he was once chosen to be.
The Hebrew text reveals something haunting in 1 Samuel 18:9:

“וַיְהִ֥י שָׁא֛וּל עֹיֵ֥ן אֶת־דָּוִ֖ד”
Vayehi Sha’ul oyen et-David

Most English translations say:
“Saul eyed David from that day forward.”
But the Hebrew word “עֹיֵן” (oyen) carries the sense of watching with hostility, suspicion, envy, and spiritual resentment.
Saul did not merely observe David.
He became consumed by him.
Because anointing exposes what titles cannot hide.
And that is where this story becomes terrifyingly personal.
There are people sitting in churches every Sunday who secretly resent the people God is raising beside them.

People who clap publicly…
while grieving privately.
People who mentor others until the student begins to surpass them.
People who celebrate your gift until heaven starts opening doors for you they prayed would open for themselves.

This is why Saul could tolerate David the shepherd…
but not David the anointed.
Before David carried oil, he was harmless.
After the anointing, he became unbearable.
And here is the painful truth most believers never talk about:
Not everyone who loves you can handle the version of you that God is calling higher.
Some only loved you when you were smaller.
When you needed them.
When you were hidden.
When your confidence was broken.
When your voice trembled.
When your gift was undeveloped.

But once God starts breathing on your life…
the atmosphere changes.
The same people who once celebrated you suddenly grow distant, cold, sarcastic, irritated, suspicious.
Why?
Because anointing reveals hearts.
Especially hidden ambition.
Especially comparison.
Especially identity wounds.
And Saul’s wounds ran deep.
When Saul was first chosen king, Scripture says he hid among the baggage.
“He was hiding himself by the baggage.” — 1 Samuel 10:22

Even before the crown…
there was insecurity.

Before authority…
there was fear.

Before leadership…
there was instability.
Saul wore armor externally because internally he never believed he was enough.
David, meanwhile, was overlooked by his own father.
Ignored by his brothers.
Forgotten in the field.
But unlike Saul, David’s identity was forged in secret places with God.
Saul needed public validation.
David survived private obscurity.

That is why one man collapsed under praise…
while the other survived persecution.
And this is where the Hebrew becomes breathtaking.
When Samuel anointed David in 1 Samuel 16:13, the text says:

“וַתִּצְלַ֞ח ר֧וּחַ יְהוָ֛ה אֶל־דָּוִ֖ד”
Vatitzlach Ruach YHWH el-David
“The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David.”
The phrase “רוּחַ יְהוָה” (Ruach YHWH) means the Spirit, breath, wind, or empowering presence of God.
But the word “תִּצְלַח” (titzlach) is explosive.

It means:
to rush,
to prosper,
to advance powerfully,
to break forth.
God’s Spirit did not casually rest on David.
It surged upon him.
And the very next verse says something devastating:
“Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul.” — 1 Samuel 16:14
One man was being filled while another was becoming empty.
Can you imagine the torment?
Saul sat on a throne heaven had already rejected.

Still wearing the crown…
while feeling God leave.

Still called “king” publicly…
while privately knowing the oil was gone.
That kind of spiritual emptiness creates desperation.
And desperate people often attack whoever reminds them of what they lost.
That is why Saul threw spears at David.
Twice.
Not because David harmed him.
But because David exposed him.
David’s presence reminded Saul that intimacy with God cannot be faked forever.
And this is the warning buried inside this story:

You can have position without presence.
Authority without intimacy.
A platform without oil.
Religion without surrender.
Saul still looked like a king.
But heaven had stopped backing him.
And some people are exhausted today because they are trying to preserve an image God already departed from.
Still pretending.
Still performing.
Still forcing.
Still manipulating.
Still trying to hold together what only repentance could heal.
But David was different.
David never chased Saul’s throne.
In fact, he repeatedly refused to kill Saul even when he had the chance.
Why?
Because David understood something modern believers often forget:
You do not need to destroy people to inherit what God promised you.

If God truly anointed you…
you can wait.
Anointing does not need sabotage to succeed.
And this is what made David terrifying to Saul.
David carried what Saul could not control.
Humility.
Purity of heart.
Dependence on God.
And eventually, Saul became mentally consumed.
The Hebrew wording in 1 Samuel 18:12 says:
“Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with him.”
Think about that.
Saul feared a man because God was near him.
Not because David had armies.
Not because David had wealth.
Not because David had political influence.
But because heaven’s presence was visible on him.
There is nothing more threatening to insecure people than someone who carries genuine intimacy with God.
Especially when no amount of striving can reproduce it.
And maybe this article is exposing something painful inside you too.
Maybe you have been secretly comparing yourself.
Secretly jealous.
Secretly wounded watching others rise while you feel forgotten.
Maybe someone else’s blessing has been tormenting your spirit.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because Saul’s story is not merely about a wicked king.
It is about what happens when identity is built on position instead of presence.
And the tragedy is this:
Saul could have repented.
He could have surrendered.
He could have humbled himself.
But pride would not let him.
The Greek Septuagint translation often uses the idea of being “troubled” or “tormented” in ways that connect deeply to inner spiritual agitation.
Not every battle is external.
Some people are losing wars nobody can see.
And envy is one of the most destructive spiritual poisons in existence because it blinds people to the grace God already gave them.
Saul forgot he was once chosen too.
And comparison always makes people forget what God already placed in their hands.
That is why this story still devastates readers thousands of years later.
Because many believers are secretly exhausted trying to compete with callings God never assigned to them.
Trying to become someone else.
Trying to force doors.
Trying to imitate another person’s oil.
Meanwhile God is saying:
“I anointed YOU for YOUR assignment.”
David never needed Saul’s identity.
And Saul never lost his throne because David stole it.
Saul lost it because disobedience slowly disconnected him from God.
That is the real tragedy.
Not David’s rise.
Saul’s refusal to repent.
And maybe somebody reading this right now has been fighting conviction for months.
Maybe your worship became performance.
Maybe your prayer life dried up.
Maybe pride has kept you from surrender.
Maybe you are still wearing a crown while privately collapsing.
But hear this carefully:
Jesus Christ restores what pride destroys.

Saul’s story ends in tragedy…
but yours does not have to.

Because where Saul resisted surrender,
Jesus embraced it.

Where Saul protected his image,
Jesus humbled Himself.

Where Saul threw spears,
Jesus stretched out His hands on the cross.
And the Gospel is this:
The same God who rejected pride still welcomes repentance.
That is why Christ came.
Not for perfect people.
But for exhausted, broken, jealous, insecure, wounded sinners who are finally ready to stop hiding.
The Hebrew word for repentance, “תשובה” (teshuvah), means to return.
Return to God.
Return to truth.
Return to surrender.
Return before pride destroys what grace was trying to heal.
And if you know someone silently struggling with comparison, jealousy, insecurity, or spiritual exhaustion, share this with them tonight.
Some people are losing battles internally while smiling externally.
Some crowns look stable in public while souls collapse in private.
